#!/bin/bash
#FLUX -N 1
#FLUX -n 1
#FLUX -q ampereq
#FLUX -t 00:10:00
#FLUX --gpus-per-task=1
#FLUX --output=para.out

# NOTE: Non-standard PBS directives ('ngpus=1', 'output=para.out') were interpreted
# and translated. Slurm environment variables and commands in the original script
# have been replaced with Flux equivalents.

module load intel-parallel-studio-xe/compilers/64
flux mini run hostname


echo Running on host `hostname`
echo Time is `date`
echo Directory is `pwd`
echo Flux job ID is $FLUX_JOB_ID
echo This job runs on the following machines:
flux exec -r all hostname | uniq
echo GPU number: $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES


module use /software/x86/tools/nvidia/hpc_sdk/modulefiles
module load nvhpc/22.9

#! Run the executable
#./d2q9-bgk input_128x128.params obstacles_128x128.dat
#./d2q9-bgk input_256x256.params obstacles_256x256.dat
#./d2q9-bgk input_1024x1024.params obstacles_1024x1024.dat
nvprof  ./parallel_scan

issues: The script loads two different compiler toolchains (Intel and NVHPC). This might cause unexpected behavior or library conflicts if the application relies on a specific environment.
The `nvprof` command is deprecated. It is recommended to use `ncu` (Nsight Compute) or `nsys` (Nsight Systems) for profiling modern CUDA applications.
The command `flux exec -r all hostname | uniq` is redundant in a single-node job (`#FLUX -N 1`), as it will produce the same output as the `hostname` command.
